statement: Let $G$ be a finite [planar graph](c:planar-graph) drawn in the plane, with a [Hamiltonian cycle](c:hamiltonian-cycle) $C$. Let $f'_k$ and $f''_k$ be the numbers of [faces](c:face) of length $k$ inside and outside $C$. Then $\sum_k (k-2)(f'_k - f''_k) = 0$.

hypotheses.text: The graph $G$ is finite, simple and drawn in the plane without crossings (a [planar graph](c:planar-graph)).
The cycle $C$ is a [Hamiltonian cycle](c:hamiltonian-cycle) of $G$: it passes once through every vertex.

conclusion: The sum $\sum_k (k-2)(f'_k - f''_k)$ over all face lengths $k$ equals $0$.

proofs.name: Face and edge count on both sides
proofs.slogan: Count the faces and the edge sides inside and outside the cycle, then subtract the two identities.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for a finite simple graph with $n \ge 3$ vertices. A graph whose face lengths break the equation has no Hamiltonian cycle, which is how the theorem is used.

roles.why: The drawing without crossings makes the faces well defined and lets the Jordan curve theorem split them into two sides.
The cycle $C$ holds all $n$ vertices, so every other edge is a chord of $C$ with both ends on $C$.

steps.slogan: Split the faces and the remaining edges into those inside and those outside $C$.
steps.detail: The cycle $C$ is a [Jordan curve](c:jordan-curve), so it separates the plane into an inside and an outside. Every [face](c:face) and every edge off $C$ lies on one side. An edge off $C$ is a chord, because all vertices lie on $C$.

steps.slogan: Count the inside faces by adding the inside chords one at a time.
steps.detail: Let $d'$ be the number of inside chords. The inside of $C$ is one face, and each new chord crosses no earlier chord, so it joins two boundary vertices of one face and cuts it in two. Hence there are $d'+1$ inside faces.

steps.slogan: Count the edge sides that bound the inside faces.
steps.detail: Each edge of $C$ bounds exactly one inside face, and each inside chord bounds two. So $\sum_k k f'_k = n + 2d'$, where $n$ is the number of edges of $C$.

steps.slogan: Combine the two counts into the inside identity $\sum_k (k-2) f'_k = n-2$.
steps.detail: Subtract twice the face count from the edge-side count: $\sum_k k f'_k - 2\sum_k f'_k = n + 2d' - 2(d'+1) = n - 2$.

steps.slogan: Repeat both counts outside $C$ to get $\sum_k (k-2) f''_k = n-2$.
steps.detail: On the sphere the outside of $C$ is also a disk, and the outside chords are added the same way. With $d''$ outside chords there are $d''+1$ outside faces and $n + 2d''$ edge sides, so the same subtraction gives $n-2$.

steps.slogan: Subtract the outside identity from the inside identity.
steps.detail: Both sums equal $n-2$, so $\sum_k (k-2)f'_k - \sum_k (k-2) f''_k = \sum_k (k-2)(f'_k - f''_k) = 0$.

concepts.c:planar-graph: A crossing-free drawing is what gives the graph faces and two sides of $C$.
concepts.c:hamiltonian-cycle: The cycle through all vertices turns every other edge into a chord.
concepts.c:face: The faces are the objects counted on each side of $C$.
concepts.c:jordan-curve: The Jordan curve theorem gives the inside and the outside of $C$.

source.note: The counting argument of E. Ja. Grinberg (Latvian Math. Yearbook 4, 1968), written without Euler's formula.

statement: Let $\varphi_1, \varphi_2$ be scalar fields that satisfy the [Wightman axioms](c:wightman-axioms), with vacuum vectors $\Omega_1, \Omega_2$. Let $U$ be a [unitary operator](c:unitary-operator) with $U\Omega_1 = \Omega_2$ that carries $\varphi_1, \dot\varphi_1$ at time $0$ to $\varphi_2, \dot\varphi_2$. Then $\varphi_1$ and $\varphi_2$ have the same two-point function.

hypotheses.text: The fields $\varphi_1, \varphi_2$ are scalar fields on Hilbert spaces $H_1, H_2$ that satisfy the [Wightman axioms](c:wightman-axioms), with Poincaré-invariant vacua $\Omega_1, \Omega_2$.

A [unitary operator](c:unitary-operator) $U\colon H_1 \to H_2$ satisfies $U\varphi_1(0,\mathbf{x})U^{-1} = \varphi_2(0,\mathbf{x})$ and the same for the time derivatives $\dot\varphi_i(0,\mathbf{x})$.
The operator $U$ maps $\Omega_1$ to $\Omega_2$, up to a phase.

conclusion: The vacuum two-point functions of $\varphi_1$ and $\varphi_2$ agree at all points, so a [free field](c:free-field) $\varphi_1$ of mass $m$ forces $\varphi_2$ to be a free field of mass $m$.

proofs.name: Equal-time equality and analytic continuation
proofs.slogan: Equality of the two fields at time zero gives equal two-point functions at spacelike points, and analyticity extends it to all points.
proofs.scope: An outline of the Hall-Wightman proof; the analytic estimates stay in the cited work. The hypothesis says that the representations of the [canonical commutation relations](c:canonical-commutation-relation) at time $0$ are unitarily equivalent; Hall and Wightman also show equality of the four-point functions.

roles.why: Poincaré invariance and the spectral condition give invariant two-point functions that are boundary values of analytic functions.
The unitary map turns the equal-time fields of one theory into those of the other.
A common vacuum makes the two vacuum expectation values at time $0$ comparable.

steps.slogan: Transfer the unitary relation at time zero to vacuum expectation values.
steps.detail: Because $U\Omega_1 = \Omega_2$ and $U$ conjugates $\varphi_1(0,\mathbf{x})$ into $\varphi_2(0,\mathbf{x})$, the products of equal-time fields have equal vacuum expectation values. In particular $\langle\Omega_1, \varphi_1(0,\mathbf{x})\varphi_1(0,\mathbf{y})\Omega_1\rangle = \langle\Omega_2, \varphi_2(0,\mathbf{x})\varphi_2(0,\mathbf{y})\Omega_2\rangle$.

steps.slogan: Boost every spacelike separation to an equal-time separation.
steps.detail: By translation invariance each two-point function is a function $W_i(\xi)$ of $\xi = x-y$. Every spacelike $\xi$ is a Lorentz transform of a purely spatial one, and $W_i$ is Lorentz invariant, so $W_1 = W_2$ on all spacelike points.

steps.slogan: Continue the equality from the spacelike points into the forward tube.
steps.detail: By the spectral condition, $W_i$ is the boundary value of a holomorphic function on a [tube domain](c:tube-domain), the forward tube. Two such functions with equal boundary values on an open set of real points agree on the whole tube, so $W_1 = W_2$ everywhere.

steps.slogan: Compare the spectral measures and use the Jost-Schroer theorem.
steps.detail: Equal two-point functions have the same Källén-Lehmann spectral measure. If $\varphi_1$ is free of mass $m$, that measure sits at $m^2$, and the Jost-Schroer theorem makes $\varphi_2$ a free field of mass $m$. So a field with the same equal-time data as a free field cannot be interacting, and the interaction picture on the [Fock space](c:fock-space) of the free field fails.

concepts.c:wightman-axioms: The axioms supply Poincaré invariance, the spectral condition and analytic Wightman functions.
concepts.c:unitary-operator: The unitary operator is the hypothetical link between the free and the interacting theory.
concepts.c:free-field: A free field has an explicit two-point function that the conclusion compares with.
concepts.c:canonical-commutation-relation: The equal-time fields represent these relations, and the hypothesis equates the two representations.
concepts.c:tube-domain: The forward tube is the domain where Wightman functions are holomorphic.
concepts.c:fock-space: The free field acts on Fock space, which the theorem shows cannot carry an interacting field.

source.ref: R. Hall and A. S. Wightman, A theorem on invariant analytic functions with applications to relativistic quantum field theory, Mat.-Fys. Medd. Danske Vid. Selsk. 31 (1957), no. 5; after R. Haag, On quantum field theories, Mat.-Fys. Medd. Danske Vid. Selsk. 29 (1955), no. 12
source.note: Also presented in Streater and Wightman, PCT, Spin and Statistics, and All That (1964), in the section on Haag's theorem.

statement: Consider the symmetries of the [S-matrix](c:s-matrix) of a four-dimensional quantum field theory under the Coleman-Mandula assumptions, but allow commuting and anticommuting generators that form a [Lie superalgebra](c:lie-superalgebra). Then the commuting part is the Poincaré algebra with a compact internal algebra and central charges, and the anticommuting generators are spin-$\tfrac12$ supercharges with $\{Q, \bar Q\} \propto P$.

hypotheses.text: The [S-matrix](c:s-matrix) is Poincaré invariant, with a mass gap, finitely many particle types of each mass and analytic scattering amplitudes (the Coleman-Mandula assumptions).
The symmetry generators form a [Lie superalgebra](c:lie-superalgebra) with commuting and anticommuting generators that act on the one-particle states.

conclusion: The commuting generators are the Poincaré algebra, a [compact Lie algebra](c:compact-lie-algebra) of internal symmetries and [central charges](c:central-charge), and the anticommuting generators are spin-$\tfrac12$ supercharges with $\{Q, \bar Q\} \propto P$, so the only nontrivial mixing is supersymmetry.

proofs.name: Coleman-Mandula, spin and Jacobi identities
proofs.slogan: Apply Coleman-Mandula to the commuting part, restrict the anticommuting generators to spin one half, and fix their brackets by the Jacobi identities.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof, which rests on the Coleman-Mandula theorem and on the physical assumptions of $S$-matrix theory. The family includes the Coleman-Mandula theorem itself, which is the case without anticommuting generators.

roles.why: These assumptions are exactly what the Coleman-Mandula theorem needs for the commuting part and for the anticommutators.
The graded structure makes each anticommutator a commuting generator that the first step already classified.

steps.slogan: Classify the commuting generators by the Coleman-Mandula theorem.
steps.detail: The commuting part is an ordinary Lie algebra of symmetries of the [S-matrix](c:s-matrix). By the Coleman-Mandula theorem it is the Poincaré algebra plus a [compact Lie algebra](c:compact-lie-algebra) of internal symmetries, whose charges are Lorentz scalars.

steps.slogan: Restrict the anticommuting generators to spin-one-half spinors.
steps.detail: The anticommuting generators form finite-dimensional representations of the [Lorentz group](c:lorentz-group). Their anticommutators are commuting generators, which step 1 allows to be only Poincaré or internal charges, and this leaves the representations $(\tfrac12,0)$ and $(0,\tfrac12)$.

steps.slogan: Identify the anticommutator of a supercharge and its conjugate with the momentum.
steps.detail: The anticommutator $\{Q, \bar Q\}$ transforms as a vector, and the only vector generator is $P_\mu$. Positivity of the norm makes the coefficient matrix positive definite, so a change of basis gives $\{Q^i_\alpha, \bar Q_{j\dot\beta}\} = 2\delta^i_j\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\beta}P_\mu$.

steps.slogan: Fix the remaining brackets by the Jacobi identities.
steps.detail: The Jacobi identities give $[P, Q] = 0$, and they make $\{Q, Q\}$ a combination of [central charges](c:central-charge) that commute with all generators. The internal algebra acts on the index $i$ and keeps the form of $\{Q, \bar Q\}$, which gives the R-symmetry.

steps.slogan: Collect the brackets into the supersymmetry algebra.
steps.detail: Steps 1 to 4 list all brackets: the Poincaré algebra, the internal algebra with central charges, and the supercharges. So the only nontrivial way to mix spacetime and internal symmetries is supersymmetry.

concepts.c:s-matrix: The theorem classifies the symmetries of the S-matrix.
concepts.c:lie-superalgebra: Commuting and anticommuting generators together form a Lie superalgebra.
concepts.c:compact-lie-algebra: Positivity of the norm restricts the internal symmetry algebra to a compact one.
concepts.c:central-charge: Central charges appear in $\{Q, Q\}$ and commute with all generators.
concepts.c:lorentz-group: Anticommuting generators transform in spinor representations of the Lorentz group.

source.ref: R. Haag, J. T. Lopuszanski and M. Sohnius, All possible generators of supersymmetries of the S-matrix, Nuclear Physics B 88 (1975), 257-274
source.note: Textbook presentation: S. Weinberg, The Quantum Theory of Fields, Volume III, Cambridge University Press (2000), section 25.2.

statement: Let $a_n \ge 0$ for all $n$, and suppose the [Abel summation](c:abel-summation) satisfies $\sum_{n\ge0} a_n e^{-ny} \sim 1/y$ as $y \downarrow 0$. Then the [partial sums](c:partial-sum) satisfy $\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k \sim n$ as $n \to \infty$.

hypotheses.text: The terms satisfy $a_n \ge 0$ for every $n$.
The [Abel summation](c:abel-summation) satisfies $\sum_{n\ge0} a_n e^{-ny} \sim 1/y$ as $y \downarrow 0$.

conclusion: The [partial sums](c:partial-sum) satisfy $\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k \sim n$, that is, the ratio to $n$ tends to $1$.

proofs.name: Karamata's polynomial approximation
proofs.slogan: Test the Abel hypothesis on monomials, extend to polynomials and continuous functions, then sandwich a jump function to read off the partial sums.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. Only the values $y = 1/N$ for integers $N$ are used in the last step, and the hypothesis $a_n \ge 0$ is what allows the sandwich.

roles.why: The asymptotic of the Abel sums gives the limit for each monomial weight.
Nonnegative terms make the weighted sums monotone in the weight function, which allows error bounds and the sandwich.

steps.slogan: Compute the weighted Abel sums for the monomials $t^k$.
steps.detail: Put $x = e^{-y}$ and $f(x) = \sum a_n x^n \sim 1/(1-x)$ as $x \uparrow 1$. Then $(1-x)\sum_n a_n x^n x^{kn} = (1-x) f(x^{k+1}) \to 1/(k+1) = \int_0^1 t^k\,dt$, because $1 - x^{k+1} \sim (k+1)(1-x)$.

steps.slogan: Extend the limit to all polynomials by linearity.
steps.detail: The sum $(1-x)\sum_n a_n x^n P(x^n)$ is linear in $P$. So for every polynomial $P$ it tends to $\int_0^1 P(t)\,dt$ as $x \uparrow 1$.

steps.slogan: Extend the limit to continuous functions by Weierstrass approximation.
steps.detail: For continuous $g$ and $\varepsilon > 0$ choose a polynomial $P$ with $|g - P| \le \varepsilon$ on $[0,1]$. As $a_n \ge 0$, the weighted sum of $g - P$ is at most $\varepsilon(1-x)f(x) \to \varepsilon$ in size, and $|\int_0^1 (g-P)| \le \varepsilon$. So the limit holds for $g$.

steps.slogan: Sandwich the jump function $\chi$ between continuous functions.
steps.detail: Let $\chi(t) = 1/t$ on $[e^{-1}, 1]$ and $\chi(t) = 0$ on $[0, e^{-1})$. For $\varepsilon > 0$ pick continuous $g_1 \le \chi \le g_2$ with $\int_0^1 (g_2 - g_1) < \varepsilon$. Since $a_n \ge 0$, the sums for $g_1, g_2$ bound the sum for $\chi$, so it tends to $\int_0^1 \chi = 1$.

steps.slogan: Set $x = e^{-1/N}$ to read off the partial sum.
steps.detail: For $x = e^{-1/N}$ we have $x^n \ge e^{-1}$ exactly when $n \le N$, and then $x^n\chi(x^n) = 1$. So $\sum_n a_n x^n\chi(x^n) = \sum_{n \le N} a_n$, while $1 - x \sim 1/N$. Hence $\frac1N\sum_{n\le N} a_n \to 1$.

concepts.c:abel-summation: The hypothesis is an asymptotic statement about Abel sums, which the proof tests on weight functions.
concepts.c:partial-sum: The conclusion is the partial sum, read off at $x = e^{-1/N}$.

source.note: Karamata's proof (1930), as presented in Hardy, Divergent Series (1949), and in Korevaar, Tauberian Theory (Springer, 2004).

statement: Let $C$ be a nonsingular [real algebraic curve](c:real-algebraic-curve) of degree $m \ge 1$ in the [real projective plane](c:real-projective-plane). Its number $c$ of [connected components](c:connected-component) satisfies $\frac{1-(-1)^m}{2} \le c \le \frac{(m-1)(m-2)}{2} + 1$.

hypotheses.text: The curve is the real zero set of a real homogeneous polynomial $F$ of degree $m$ in three variables, in the [real projective plane](c:real-projective-plane).
The curve $F = 0$ has no singular point over $\mathbb{C}$.

conclusion: The number $c$ of [connected components](c:connected-component) of the real curve lies between $\frac{1-(-1)^m}{2}$ and $\frac{(m-1)(m-2)}{2} + 1$.

proofs.name: Bezout with an interpolating curve
proofs.slogan: Pass a curve of degree $m-2$ through chosen points of many components and count its intersections with Bezout's theorem.
proofs.scope: Odd degree gives the lower bound by a real line; the upper bound is proved for $m \ge 3$ by contradiction, and for $m \le 2$ the curve is a line, a circle or empty. The bound $\frac{(m-1)(m-2)}{2} + 1$ is one more than the [genus](c:genus-of-a-surface) of the complex curve; sharpness is not proved here.

roles.why: A real equation gives a real interpolating curve $D$ and a sign for $F$ along each component.
A nonsingular plane curve is irreducible and its intersection multiplicity with $D$ is the order of vanishing along the curve.

steps.slogan: Find a real point on a curve of odd degree.
steps.detail: A real line $L$ meets the complex curve in $m$ points, counted with [multiplicity](c:intersection-multiplicity), by Bezout's theorem. Non-real points come in conjugate pairs, so odd $m$ leaves a real point and $c \ge 1$. For even $m$ the lower bound is $0$.

steps.slogan: Choose points on the ovals, assuming that there are too many components.
steps.detail: Let $g = \frac{(m-1)(m-2)}{2}$ and suppose $c \ge g+2$. Components are ovals, except at most one one-sided component when $m$ is odd. For odd $m$ choose one point on each of $g$ ovals and $m-2$ points on another oval; for even $m$ choose one point on each of $g+1$ ovals and $m-3$ on another.

steps.slogan: Fit a real curve $D$ of degree $m-2$ through the chosen points.
steps.detail: Both choices give $g + m - 2 = \frac{(m-2)(m+1)}{2}$ points. Real curves of degree $m-2$ form a projective space of dimension $\frac{(m-2)(m+1)}{2}$, so a real curve $D$ passes through all chosen points.

steps.slogan: Show that $D$ meets each oval in an even number of points.
steps.detail: Lift an oval to a closed curve $\gamma$ on $S^2$. Because $C$ is nonsingular, the multiplicity of $D \cap C$ at $\gamma(t)$ is the order of vanishing of $F_D \circ \gamma$, and it is odd exactly where $F_D$ changes sign. A function on a circle changes sign an even number of times, so the total multiplicity on an oval is even.

steps.slogan: Count the intersections and contradict Bezout's bound $m(m-2)$.
steps.detail: The curves $C$ and $D$ share no component, since $C$ is irreducible and $\deg D < m$. By the parity step each oval holding a chosen point meets $D$ at least twice, and an oval with $m-2$ or $m-3$ chosen points meets it at least $m-2$ times (odd $m$: $m-1$). The total is at least $m^2 - 2m + 1 > m(m-2)$, against Bezout's theorem.

steps.slogan: Combine the contradiction and the real line into the two bounds.
steps.detail: The contradiction gives $c \le g + 1 = \frac{(m-1)(m-2)}{2} + 1$ for $m \ge 3$. Together with the lower bound of step 1, and the direct cases $m \le 2$, this gives the stated range.

concepts.c:real-algebraic-curve: The theorem bounds the topology of the real points of such a curve.
concepts.c:real-projective-plane: The curve lives in the real projective plane, where lines always meet.
concepts.c:connected-component: The components of the real curve are what the proof counts.
concepts.c:genus-of-a-surface: The upper bound equals the genus of the complex curve plus one.
concepts.c:intersection-multiplicity: Bezout's theorem counts intersection points with these multiplicities.

source.note: Harnack's Bezout argument (Math. Ann. 10 (1876), 189-198), rewritten with the sign-change count for parity.

statement: Let $S$ be a complete surface of constant negative [Gaussian curvature](c:gaussian-curvature). Then there is no isometric [immersion](c:immersion) of $S$ into $\mathbb{R}^3$. In particular no complete [regular surface](c:regular-surface) in $\mathbb{R}^3$ has constant negative curvature.

hypotheses.text: The surface $S$ is a complete Riemannian surface (geodesically complete).
The [Gaussian curvature](c:gaussian-curvature) of $S$ is a negative constant $K$.

proofs.name: Asymptotic coordinates and area
proofs.slogan: An immersed complete surface of curvature $-1$ would be the hyperbolic plane covered by asymptotic coordinates whose squares have area less than $2\pi$.
proofs.scope: An outline by contradiction: assume an isometric immersion exists. After scaling, $K = -1$, and the technical lemma on global asymptotic coordinates is cited from do Carmo.

roles.why: Completeness makes $\exp_p$ a covering and lets the asymptotic coordinates run over all of $\mathbb{R}^2$.
Negative curvature gives two asymptotic directions and the relation $\theta_{uv} = \sin\theta$ for the angle $\theta$ between them.

steps.slogan: Rescale to $K = -1$ and lift to the hyperbolic plane.
steps.detail: Scaling gives $K \equiv -1$. For complete $S$ with $K \le 0$, $\exp_p \colon T_pS \to S$ is a covering, so the pulled back metric on $\mathbb{R}^2$ is complete with $K \equiv -1$, the [hyperbolic plane](c:hyperbolic-plane) $H$. The composite $H \to S \to \mathbb{R}^3$ is an isometric immersion.

steps.slogan: Take the asymptotic curves of the immersion as coordinate curves.
steps.detail: Because $K < 0$, each point has two distinct asymptotic directions. Locally the asymptotic curves give coordinates $(u,v)$ with $E = G = 1$, $F = \cos\theta$ and $0 < \theta < \pi$, and the Gauss equation gives $\theta_{uv} = \sin\theta$ for $K = -1$.

steps.slogan: Show that every asymptotic quadrilateral has area less than $2\pi$.
steps.detail: The area of $[u_0,u_1] \times [v_0,v_1]$ is $\iint \sin\theta\,du\,dv = \iint \theta_{uv}\,du\,dv = \theta_{11} + \theta_{00} - \theta_{10} - \theta_{01}$. Each angle lies in $(0,\pi)$, so the sum is less than $2\pi$.

steps.slogan: Extend the asymptotic coordinates to a diffeomorphism from $\mathbb{R}^2$ onto $H$.
steps.detail: The cited lemmas of do Carmo use completeness of $H$ to extend the coordinates along asymptotic curves to all of $\mathbb{R}^2$. They show that the resulting map $x\colon \mathbb{R}^2 \to H$ is a diffeomorphism, so $H$ has a global asymptotic parametrization.

steps.slogan: Compare the bounded area of squares with the infinite area of $H$.
steps.detail: The squares $[-n,n]^2$ exhaust $H$ and each has image of area less than $2\pi$, so $H$ has area at most $2\pi$. But a disc of radius $r$ in $H$ has area $2\pi(\cosh r - 1) \to \infty$. This contradiction shows that no immersion exists.

concepts.c:gaussian-curvature: Constant negative curvature fixes the hyperbolic metric and the asymptotic net.
concepts.c:immersion: The assumed immersion is what supplies the asymptotic curves.
concepts.c:regular-surface: A complete regular surface in space is the special case of an immersed one.
concepts.c:hyperbolic-plane: The lifted surface is the hyperbolic plane, which has infinite area.

source.ref: M. P. do Carmo, Differential Geometry of Curves and Surfaces, Prentice-Hall, 1976, section 5-11; original: D. Hilbert, Ueber Flaechen von constanter Gaussscher Kruemmung, Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 2 (1901), 87-99
source.note: The steps follow do Carmo's proof by asymptotic coordinates.

statement: Let $ABC$ and $A'B'C'$ be [triangles](c:triangle) with $AB = A'B'$ and $AC = A'C'$. If the [angle](c:angle) at $A$ is larger than the angle at $A'$, then $BC > B'C'$.

hypotheses.text: Two sides of the first triangle equal two sides of the second: $AB = A'B'$ and $AC = A'C'$.
The included [angle](c:angle) at $A$ is larger than the included angle at $A'$.

conclusion: The third side of the first triangle is longer: $BC > B'C'$.

proofs.name: Law of cosines
proofs.slogan: Write both third sides by the law of cosines and compare them through the strictly decreasing cosine.
proofs.scope: Non-degenerate triangles, with angles in $(0,\pi)$. This is the algebraic proof; Euclid's own proof (Elements I.24) is by construction.

roles.why: The two equal side pairs make the formulas for $BC^2$ and $B'C'^2$ differ only in the cosine.
A larger angle in $(0,\pi)$ has a smaller [cosine](c:cosine).

steps.slogan: Write each third side by the law of cosines.
steps.detail: Let $b = AC = A'C'$ and $c = AB = A'B'$. The law of cosines gives $BC^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc\cos A$ and $B'C'^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc\cos A'$.

steps.slogan: Compare the cosines of the two included angles.
steps.detail: The [cosine](c:cosine) is strictly decreasing on $[0,\pi]$, and both angles lie in $(0,\pi)$. From $A > A'$ we get $\cos A < \cos A'$.

steps.slogan: Subtract the two formulas to compare the squared sides.
steps.detail: We have $BC^2 - B'C'^2 = 2bc(\cos A' - \cos A)$. Here $b, c > 0$ and $\cos A' - \cos A > 0$, so $BC^2 > B'C'^2$.

steps.slogan: Take positive square roots of the squared sides.
steps.detail: Lengths are positive and $x \mapsto \sqrt{x}$ is increasing, so $BC^2 > B'C'^2$ gives $BC > B'C'$.

concepts.c:triangle: The theorem compares the third sides of two triangles.
concepts.c:angle: The included angle decides which third side is longer.
concepts.c:cosine: Strict monotonicity of cosine turns the angle inequality into a length inequality.

source.note: The standard trigonometric proof from the law of cosines; Euclid, Elements, Book I, Proposition 24 proves it by construction.

statement: Let $s$ be a finite index set, let $w_i > 0$ with $\sum_{i\in s} w_i = 1$, and let $z_i > 0$. Then the [weighted](c:weighted-mean) harmonic mean is at most the weighted geometric mean: $\big(\sum_{i \in s} w_i/z_i\big)^{-1} \le \prod_{i \in s} z_i^{w_i}$.

hypotheses.text: The weights satisfy $w_i > 0$ for every $i$ and $\sum_{i\in s} w_i = 1$.
The values satisfy $z_i > 0$ for every $i$.

conclusion: The inequality $\big(\sum_{i \in s} w_i/z_i\big)^{-1} \le \prod_{i \in s} z_i^{w_i}$ holds.

formal.difference: mathlib also assumes that the index set is nonempty, which follows from the weights summing to $1$. The statements agree otherwise.

proofs.name: AM-GM for the reciprocals
proofs.slogan: Apply the weighted AM-GM inequality to the reciprocals $1/z_i$ and invert both sides.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, with the same weights. The index set is nonempty because the weights sum to $1$.

roles.why: Positive weights with sum $1$ are the weights that weighted AM-GM needs, and they make the sum positive.
Positive $z_i$ give positive reciprocals for AM-GM and let the real powers and the inverses exist.

steps.slogan: Put the reciprocals $1/z_i$ into the weighted AM-GM inequality.
steps.detail: The numbers $1/z_i$ are positive, and the weights are positive with sum $1$. Weighted AM-GM gives $\prod_i (1/z_i)^{w_i} \le \sum_i w_i/z_i$.

steps.slogan: Check that both sides of the AM-GM inequality are positive.
steps.detail: A product of positive reals raised to real powers is positive. The sum $\sum_i w_i/z_i$ is a nonempty sum of positive terms, so it is positive.

steps.slogan: Invert both positive sides to reverse the inequality.
steps.detail: For positive $a \le b$ we have $b^{-1} \le a^{-1}$. So $\big(\sum_i w_i/z_i\big)^{-1} \le \big(\prod_i (1/z_i)^{w_i}\big)^{-1}$.

steps.slogan: Rewrite the inverted product as $\prod_i z_i^{w_i}$.
steps.detail: For $z > 0$ and real $w$ we have $(1/z)^w = (z^w)^{-1}$. Hence $\big(\prod_i (1/z_i)^{w_i}\big)^{-1} = \prod_i z_i^{w_i}$, which is the right side.

concepts.c:weighted-mean: The statement compares two weighted means that use the same weights.

source.note: mathlib applies Real.geom_mean_le_arith_mean_weighted to $1/z_i$, then inverts with inv_le_inv₀ and Finset.prod_inv_distrib.

statement: Let $U$ be an open convex subset of a [Banach space](c:banach-space) $X$, and let $f\colon U \to \mathbb{R}$ be [Fréchet differentiable](c:frechet-derivative). Then $f$ is a [convex function](c:convex-function) if and only if $f'$ is a [monotone operator](c:monotone-operator): $\langle f'(x) - f'(y), x - y\rangle \ge 0$ for all $x, y \in U$.

hypotheses.text: The set $U$ is an open convex subset of a [Banach space](c:banach-space) $X$.
The function $f\colon U \to \mathbb{R}$ is [Fréchet differentiable](c:frechet-derivative) at every point of $U$.

conclusion: The function $f$ is [convex](c:convex-function) exactly when $\langle f'(x) - f'(y), x - y\rangle \ge 0$ for all $x, y \in U$.

proofs.name: Gradient inequality and segments
proofs.slogan: Convexity gives the gradient inequality, whose two copies add to monotonicity; conversely monotonicity makes the derivative along a segment nondecreasing.
proofs.scope: Both implications, for any real-valued $f$ on $U$. The proof never uses completeness of $X$, so it holds on any normed space.

roles.why: Convexity of $U$ keeps the segments inside $U$, and openness gives an interval around $[0,1]$ for differentiation.
The Fréchet derivative gives the one-sided limit in the gradient inequality and the chain rule along a segment.

steps.slogan: Derive the gradient inequality from [convexity](c:convex-function).
steps.detail: For $t \in (0,1]$ convexity gives $\frac{f(x + t(y-x)) - f(x)}{t} \le f(y) - f(x)$. Letting $t \to 0^+$, the [Fréchet derivative](c:frechet-derivative) gives $\langle f'(x), y - x\rangle \le f(y) - f(x)$.

steps.slogan: Add the gradient inequalities for $(x,y)$ and $(y,x)$.
steps.detail: We have $f(y) \ge f(x) + \langle f'(x), y-x\rangle$ and $f(x) \ge f(y) + \langle f'(y), x-y\rangle$. Adding them gives $0 \ge -\langle f'(x) - f'(y), x-y\rangle$, which is [monotonicity](c:monotone-operator).

steps.slogan: Restrict $f$ to a segment to get a function of one variable.
steps.detail: Fix $x, y \in U$ and put $z_t = x + t(y-x)$ and $\varphi(t) = f(z_t)$ for $t$ in an open interval around $[0,1]$. The chain rule gives $\varphi'(t) = \langle f'(z_t), y-x\rangle$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\varphi'$ is nondecreasing when $f'$ is monotone.
steps.detail: For $s < t$ we have $z_t - z_s = (t-s)(y-x)$. So $\varphi'(t) - \varphi'(s) = \frac{1}{t-s}\langle f'(z_t) - f'(z_s), z_t - z_s\rangle \ge 0$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $\varphi$ is convex, so $f$ is convex.
steps.detail: For $0 < t < 1$ the mean value theorem gives $\xi_1 < t < \xi_2$ with $\varphi(t) - \varphi(0) = t\varphi'(\xi_1)$ and $\varphi(1) - \varphi(t) = (1-t)\varphi'(\xi_2)$. Since $\varphi'(\xi_1) \le \varphi'(\xi_2)$, we get $\varphi(t) \le (1-t)\varphi(0) + t\varphi(1)$, which says $f(z_t) \le (1-t)f(x) + tf(y)$.

steps.slogan: Join the two implications into the equivalence.
steps.detail: Steps 1 and 2 show that convexity gives monotonicity. Steps 3 to 5 show that monotonicity gives convexity. Together $f$ is convex if and only if $f'$ is monotone.

concepts.c:banach-space: The space only supplies the norm and the dual pairing for the derivative.
concepts.c:frechet-derivative: The derivative gives the gradient inequality and the chain rule along a segment.
concepts.c:convex-function: Convexity is one side of the equivalence and is tested along segments.
concepts.c:monotone-operator: Monotonicity of $f'$ is the other side of the equivalence.

source.note: The standard argument for gradient monotonicity; the theorem is due to R. I. Kachurovskii (1960).

statement: Let $\lambda\colon \Sigma^\infty \mathbb{R}P^\infty \to S^0$ be the [transfer map](c:transfer-map) of the double cover $S^\infty \to \mathbb{R}P^\infty$. For every $n \ge 1$, the induced map $\pi_n^s(\mathbb{R}P^\infty) \to \pi_n^s(S^0)$ of [stable homotopy groups](c:stable-homotopy-groups) is onto the $2$-primary part of $\pi_n^s(S^0)$.

hypotheses.text: The map $\lambda$ is the stable [transfer map](c:transfer-map) of the double cover $S^\infty \to \mathbb{R}P^\infty$, from [real projective space](c:real-projective-space) to the sphere spectrum.
The degree $n$ is at least $1$.

conclusion: Every element of the $2$-primary part of $\pi_n^s(S^0)$ is $\lambda_*(\alpha)$ for some $\alpha \in \pi_n^s(\mathbb{R}P^\infty)$.

proofs.name: Transfer as an infinite loop map
proofs.slogan: Build the transfer, make it an infinite loop map, prove surjectivity for finite complexes, and specialize to spheres.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof; the analysis of the infinite loop map stays in the cited work. The theorem is the sphere case of surjectivity for all connected finite $2$-primary complexes.

roles.why: The transfer of the double cover gives the stable map that becomes the infinite loop map.
Degree zero is excluded because $\pi_0^s(S^0)$ is $\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{R}P^\infty$ is connected.

steps.slogan: Construct the stable transfer of the double cover $S^\infty \to \mathbb{R}P^\infty$.
steps.detail: The cited work builds a stable transfer for finite covers. For the double cover $E\Sigma_2 \to B\Sigma_2$ it gives a stable map $\Sigma^\infty \mathbb{R}P^\infty_+ \to S^0$, and its restriction is $\lambda$.

steps.slogan: Promote the stable map to a map of infinite loop spaces.
steps.detail: Applying $\Omega^\infty$ gives an infinite loop map $Q\mathbb{R}P^\infty \to Q_0 S^0$, where $Q = \Omega^\infty\Sigma^\infty$ and $Q_0 S^0$ is the degree zero component. It extends the map $\mathbb{R}P^\infty \to Q_0S^0$ and induces $\lambda_*$ on homotopy groups.

steps.slogan: Prove surjectivity of $[X, \lambda]$ for connected finite $2$-primary complexes $X$.
steps.detail: The cited paper analyses the effect of $\lambda$ as an infinite loop map. It shows that $[X, Q\mathbb{R}P^\infty] \to [X, Q_0S^0]$ is onto for every connected finite $2$-primary CW complex $X$.

steps.slogan: Specialize to spheres to get surjectivity on stable homotopy groups.
steps.detail: Take $X = S^n$ with $n \ge 1$, which is connected. Then $\pi_n(Q\mathbb{R}P^\infty) = \pi_n^s(\mathbb{R}P^\infty)$ maps onto the $2$-primary part of $\pi_n(Q_0S^0) = \pi_n^s(S^0)$.

concepts.c:transfer-map: The transfer map is the stable map whose surjectivity the theorem states.
concepts.c:stable-homotopy-groups: The theorem is a surjectivity statement about these groups.
concepts.c:real-projective-space: The infinite real projective space is the source of the transfer.

source.ref: D. S. Kahn and S. B. Priddy, The transfer and stable homotopy theory, Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society 83 (1978), 103-111; announced in Applications of the transfer to stable homotopy theory, Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society 78 (1972), 981-987
source.note: The Mahowald-Whitehead conjecture, proved by Kahn and Priddy.

statement: If [SAT](c:boolean-satisfiability-problem) has polynomial-size [Boolean circuits](c:boolean-circuit), that is $\mathsf{NP} \subseteq \mathsf{P/poly}$, then $\Pi_2^p = \Sigma_2^p$, and the [polynomial hierarchy](c:polynomial-hierarchy) collapses: $\mathsf{PH} = \Sigma_2^p$.

hypotheses.text: There are [Boolean circuits](c:boolean-circuit) $C_n$ of size polynomial in $n$ that decide [SAT](c:boolean-satisfiability-problem) on formulas of size $n$.

proofs.name: Guess the search circuit
proofs.slogan: Turn the decision circuits into search circuits, guess one existentially, and check it against all universal inputs.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The step from $\Pi_2^p \subseteq \Sigma_2^p$ to $\mathsf{PH} = \Sigma_2^p$ is the usual collapse by induction.

roles.why: The circuits for SAT give search circuits, which are the small witness that the existential quantifier guesses.

steps.slogan: Turn the decision circuits into circuits that output a satisfying assignment.
steps.detail: Set the variables of a formula $\varphi$ one by one: ask the circuit $C_n$ whether $\varphi$ with $x_1 = 1$ is satisfiable, fix $x_1$ accordingly, and continue. This self-reduction gives circuits $S_n$ of polynomial size that output a satisfying assignment whenever $\varphi$ is satisfiable.

steps.slogan: Write a $\Pi_2^p$ language with a satisfiability formula for each universal input.
steps.detail: Let $x \in L \iff \forall y\,\exists z\,\psi(x,y,z)$ with $\psi$ in polynomial time. The Cook-Levin reduction gives a formula $\varphi_{x,y}$ of polynomial size, whose satisfying assignments give a $z$ with $\psi(x,y,z)$.

steps.slogan: Replace the inner quantifier by a guessed circuit and prove the equivalence.
steps.detail: Claim: $x \in L$ iff some circuit $S$ of polynomial size has $S(\varphi_{x,y})$ satisfying $\varphi_{x,y}$ for every $y$. If $x \in L$, every $\varphi_{x,y}$ is satisfiable and $S_n$ works. If such $S$ exists, each $\varphi_{x,y}$ has a satisfying assignment, so $x \in L$.

steps.slogan: Recognize the new condition as a $\Sigma_2^p$ condition.
steps.detail: The condition has the form $\exists S\,\forall y$ followed by a polynomial-time check: evaluate $S$ on $\varphi_{x,y}$ and test the answer. So $\Pi_2^p \subseteq \Sigma_2^p$. Taking complements gives $\Sigma_2^p \subseteq \Pi_2^p$.

steps.slogan: Collapse the hierarchy from the equality $\Sigma_2^p = \Pi_2^p$.
steps.detail: If $\Sigma_k^p = \Sigma_2^p$ for some $k \ge 2$, then $\Pi_k^p = \Pi_2^p = \Sigma_2^p$. So $\Sigma_{k+1}^p = \exists^p\Pi_k^p = \exists^p\Sigma_2^p = \Sigma_2^p$. By induction every level equals $\Sigma_2^p$, so $\mathsf{PH} = \Sigma_2^p$.

concepts.c:boolean-satisfiability-problem: The hypothesis gives small circuits for SAT, the NP-complete problem.
concepts.c:boolean-circuit: A guessed polynomial-size circuit is the witness that replaces the universal check.
concepts.c:polynomial-hierarchy: The collapse of this hierarchy to level two is the conclusion.

source.note: The Karp-Lipton argument (STOC 1980), as in Arora and Barak, Computational Complexity (2009), chapter 6.

statement: Let $G = (V, E)$ be a finite graph without isolated vertices, with couplings $J_{ij} \ge 0$. Let $Z(h) = \sum_{\sigma \in \{\pm1\}^V} \exp\big(\sum_{ij \in E} J_{ij}\sigma_i\sigma_j + h\sum_i \sigma_i\big)$ be the [partition function](c:partition-function) of the ferromagnetic [Ising model](c:ising-model) in a complex field $h$. Then $Z(h) \neq 0$ whenever $\operatorname{Re} h \neq 0$.

hypotheses.text: The graph $G$ is finite and has no isolated vertices.
The couplings are ferromagnetic: $J_{ij} \ge 0$ for every edge $ij$ of the [Ising model](c:ising-model).

conclusion: Every zero of the [partition function](c:partition-function) $Z$ in the field $h$ is purely imaginary.

proofs.name: Asano contraction
proofs.slogan: Build the partition function from edge polynomials with no zeros in the unit polydisc, and keep that property under contraction.
proofs.scope: The uniform field $h$; an isolated vertex only adds the factor $2\cosh h$, whose zeros are purely imaginary. The same proof gives a separate field $h_i$ at each site.

roles.why: The condition $J \ge 0$ makes the edge polynomial vanish only outside the open unit bidisc.
Finitely many edges and vertices give a polynomial in finitely many variables that contracts step by step.

steps.slogan: Show that the one-edge polynomial has no zero in the open unit bidisc.
Give each edge its own end variables and multiply the edge polynomials.
steps.detail: For each vertex $i$ and edge $e \ni i$ take a variable $z_{i,e}$, and put $P = \prod_{e = ij} f_e(z_{i,e}, z_{j,e})$. Each $f_e$ is affine in each variable, and $P$ has no zero when all variables lie in the open unit disc, as a product of nonzero factors.

steps.slogan: Bound the coefficients of a zero-free affine polynomial in two variables.
steps.detail: Let $P = A + Bz_1 + Cz_2 + Dz_1z_2$ have no zero in $|z_1|, |z_2| < 1$. For fixed $z_1$ the root in $z_2$ lies outside the disc, so $|A + Bz_1| \ge |C + Dz_1|$ for $|z_1| \le 1$. Averaging the squares over the circle gives $|A|^2 + |B|^2 \ge |C|^2 + |D|^2$.

steps.slogan: Deduce that the contraction $A + Dz$ has no zero in the open unit disc.
steps.detail: The same argument in $z_2$ gives $|A|^2 + |C|^2 \ge |B|^2 + |D|^2$. Adding the two inequalities gives $|A| \ge |D|$, and $A = P(0,0) \ne 0$. So $A + Dz \ne 0$ for $|z| < 1$, for any values of the other variables in the open disc.

steps.slogan: Contract the variables of each vertex to recover the partition function.
steps.detail: Contracting $y_1, y_2$ to $y$ keeps the terms without $y_1, y_2$ and with both, and replaces $y_1y_2$ by $y$. Doing this for all variables $z_{i,e}$ of vertex $i$ keeps the terms where all edges at $i$ choose the same spin $\sigma_i$. The result is $\sum_\sigma \prod_e e^{J_e\sigma_i\sigma_j}\prod_i z_i^{(1+\sigma_i)/2}$, which has no zero when all $|z_i| < 1$.

steps.slogan: Set $z_i = e^{2h}$ and use the spin-flip symmetry.
steps.detail: Since $e^{h\sum\sigma_i} = e^{-nh}\prod_i (e^{2h})^{(1+\sigma_i)/2}$ with $n = |V|$, we get $Z(h) \ne 0$ when $|e^{2h}| < 1$, that is $\operatorname{Re} h < 0$. The flip $\sigma \mapsto -\sigma$ gives $Z(h) = Z(-h)$, so $Z(h) \ne 0$ also for $\operatorname{Re} h > 0$.

concepts.c:partition-function: The partition function is the polynomial in $e^{2h}$ whose zeros the theorem locates.
concepts.c:ising-model: The Ising model supplies the edge weights $e^{J\sigma_i\sigma_j}$ and the spin-flip symmetry.

source.note: The Asano contraction proof (T. Asano 1970; D. Ruelle 1971; see Lieb and Sokal, Comm. Math. Phys. 80 (1981), 153-179) of the theorem of T. D. Lee and C. N. Yang, Phys. Rev. 87 (1952), 410-419.

statement: Let $p$ be a point of a [regular surface](c:regular-surface) $S$ with unit normal $N$. Regular curves on $S$ through $p$ with the same tangent line have the same [normal curvature](c:normal-curvature) $\kappa_n = \kappa\cos\theta$ at $p$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the principal normal and $N$. If $\kappa_n \ne 0$ their [osculating circles](c:osculating-circle) lie on one sphere.

hypotheses.text: The set $S$ is a [regular surface](c:regular-surface) with a smooth unit normal field $N$ near $p$.
The curves are $C^2$ regular curves on $S$ through $p$ that share one tangent line, with curvature $\kappa \ne 0$ at $p$ for the sphere statement.

conclusion: All these curves have the same [normal curvature](c:normal-curvature) at $p$, and when it is nonzero their [osculating circles](c:osculating-circle) lie on the sphere of radius $1/|\kappa_n|$ that touches $S$ at $p$.

proofs.name: Normal component of the acceleration
proofs.slogan: Differentiate the tangency condition to show that the normal part of the acceleration depends only on the tangent, then check the sphere by direct computation.
proofs.scope: Curves with $\kappa = 0$ at $p$ have $\kappa_n = 0$ and no osculating circle, so only the first claim concerns them. The sign of $\kappa_n$ depends on the choice of $N$ but not on the direction of the tangent.

roles.why: The unit normal field gives the orthogonality $\langle\alpha', N\rangle = 0$ and the [second fundamental form](c:second-fundamental-form).
A common tangent $v$ and nonzero curvature fix the acceleration $\kappa n$ and the center of each osculating circle.

steps.slogan: Parametrize the curve by arc length with unit tangent $v$ at $p$.
steps.detail: Let $\alpha(s)$ have $\alpha(0) = p$ and $\alpha'(0) = v$, a unit vector. Then $\alpha''(0) = \kappa n$, with [curvature](c:curvature) $\kappa$ and principal normal $n$. Reversing the direction of $v$ changes neither $\kappa$ nor $n$.

steps.slogan: Differentiate the orthogonality $\langle\alpha', N\rangle = 0$ along the curve.
steps.detail: Since $\alpha$ lies on $S$, $\langle\alpha'(s), N(\alpha(s))\rangle = 0$. Differentiating at $s = 0$ gives $\langle\alpha'', N\rangle = -\langle v, dN_p(v)\rangle = \mathrm{II}_p(v,v)$, the [second fundamental form](c:second-fundamental-form) of $S$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the normal curvature depends only on the tangent line.
steps.detail: We get $\kappa\cos\theta = \langle\kappa n, N\rangle = \langle\alpha''(0), N\rangle = \mathrm{II}_p(v,v)$. This depends only on $p$ and $\pm v$, so all curves with the same tangent line have the same $\kappa_n$.

steps.slogan: Locate the center of each osculating circle.
steps.detail: The [osculating circle](c:osculating-circle) has radius $r = 1/\kappa$ and center $c = p + rn$, in the plane spanned by $v$ and $n$. By step 3, $\langle c - p, N\rangle = r\cos\theta = 1/\kappa_n =: \rho$.

steps.slogan: Show that every point of every osculating circle lies on one sphere.
steps.detail: A point of the circle is $q = p + r[(1-\cos\varphi)n + \sin\varphi\,v]$. Then $|q-p|^2 = 2r^2(1-\cos\varphi)$ and $\langle q-p, N\rangle = r(1-\cos\varphi)\cos\theta$. Since $\rho r\cos\theta = r^2$, we get $|q - p - \rho N|^2 = \rho^2$, so $q$ lies on the sphere with center $p + \rho N$ and radius $|\rho|$.

concepts.c:regular-surface: The surface carries the unit normal field and the curves.
concepts.c:normal-curvature: The normal curvature is the normal part of the curve's acceleration.
concepts.c:osculating-circle: The osculating circles are the circles shown to lie on one sphere.
concepts.c:second-fundamental-form: The normal curvature equals the second fundamental form of the tangent vector.
concepts.c:curvature: The curvature $\kappa$ gives the acceleration $\kappa n$ and the radius of the circle.

source.note: The standard computation, as in textbooks on curves and surfaces such as do Carmo, Differential Geometry of Curves and Surfaces.

statement: Let $\Phi$ be a [nuclear space](c:nuclear-space) with dual $\Phi'$, and let $\mu$ be a [cylindrical measure](c:cylindrical-measure) on $\Phi'$. If its Fourier transform (characteristic functional) $\hat\mu(f) = \int e^{i\langle\xi, f\rangle}\,d\mu(\xi)$ is continuous on $\Phi$, then $\mu$ extends to a [Radon measure](c:radon-measure) on $\Phi'$.

hypotheses.text: The space $\Phi$ is a [nuclear space](c:nuclear-space).
The measure $\mu$ is a [cylindrical](c:cylindrical-measure) probability measure on the dual $\Phi'$.
The Fourier transform $\hat\mu$ is continuous on $\Phi$.

conclusion: The cylindrical measure $\mu$ is the restriction of a [Radon measure](c:radon-measure) on $\Phi'$, which is unique.

proofs.name: Hilbert-Schmidt reduction to Sazonov
proofs.slogan: Nuclearity turns continuity of the Fourier transform into Sazonov continuity on a Hilbert space, where Sazonov's theorem gives a measure.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof. The equivalent Bochner-Minlos form says that a continuous positive definite functional $C$ on $\Phi$ with $C(0) = 1$ is the Fourier transform of a unique Radon probability measure on $\Phi'$.

roles.why: Continuity of $\hat\mu$ at $0$ bounds $1 - \hat\mu$ on the unit ball of a Hilbert seminorm.
Nuclearity supplies a larger Hilbert seminorm whose inclusion is Hilbert-Schmidt.
A cylindrical measure has consistent finite-dimensional marginals, which Sazonov's theorem upgrades to a measure.

steps.slogan: Choose a Hilbert seminorm that controls the continuity of the Fourier transform.
steps.detail: The topology of $\Phi$ is given by Hilbert seminorms. Continuity of $\hat\mu$ at $0$ gives, for each $\varepsilon > 0$, a continuous Hilbert seminorm $p$ with $|1 - \hat\mu(f)| < \varepsilon$ whenever $p(f) \le 1$.

steps.slogan: Use nuclearity to find a larger Hilbert seminorm with Hilbert-Schmidt inclusion.
steps.detail: Because $\Phi$ is nuclear, there is a continuous Hilbert seminorm $q \ge p$ such that the canonical map from the completion $H_q$ to $H_p$ is Hilbert-Schmidt.

steps.slogan: Show that the Fourier transform is continuous in the Sazonov topology of $H_q$.
steps.detail: A Sazonov neighborhood of $0$ is $\{f : \|Tf\| < 1\}$ for a Hilbert-Schmidt $T$. Take $T$ to be the map $H_q \to H_p$ of step 2. Then $\hat\mu$ is small on this neighborhood, and it extends from $\Phi$ to $H_q$ by uniform continuity.

steps.slogan: Apply Sazonov's theorem to get a Radon measure on the dual of $H_q$.
steps.detail: The cylindrical measure induced on $H_q'$ has Sazonov-continuous Fourier transform. Sazonov's theorem says that such a cylindrical measure on a Hilbert space is a Radon measure.

steps.slogan: Carry the Radon measure back to $\Phi'$ and check uniqueness.
steps.detail: The dual $H_q'$ embeds continuously in $\Phi'$, so the measure pushes forward to a Radon measure on $\Phi'$ with the marginals of $\mu$. A Radon measure is determined by its finite-dimensional marginals, so it is unique.

concepts.c:nuclear-space: Nuclearity gives the Hilbert-Schmidt inclusion that the reduction needs.
concepts.c:cylindrical-measure: The cylindrical measure is the object that is shown to be a true measure.
concepts.c:radon-measure: The Radon measure is the countably additive measure that the theorem produces.

source.ref: R. A. Minlos, Generalized random processes and their extension to a measure, Trudy Moskov. Mat. Obshch. 8 (1959), 497-518; see also I. M. Gelfand and N. Ya. Vilenkin, Generalized Functions, Vol. 4: Applications of Harmonic Analysis, Academic Press, 1964, chapter IV
source.note: The proof reduces to Sazonov's theorem through the Hilbert-Schmidt characterization of nuclear spaces.

statement: Let $X$ be a Hausdorff [locally convex space](c:locally-convex-space) with dual $X^*$. If every subseries of a [series](c:series) $\sum x_n$ in $X$ converges in the [weak topology](c:weak-topology) $\sigma(X, X^*)$, then every subseries converges in the Mackey topology $\tau(X, X^*)$.

hypotheses.text: The space $X$ is a Hausdorff [locally convex space](c:locally-convex-space) with dual $X^*$.
For every set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ the series $\sum_{n \in A} x_n$ converges in the [weak topology](c:weak-topology), to an element $x_A \in X$.

conclusion: For every $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ the series $\sum_{n\in A} x_n$ converges to $x_A$ in the Mackey topology $\tau(X, X^*)$.

proofs.name: Schur property of the sequence space
proofs.slogan: Map each weak*-compact disk of functionals into a weakly compact subset of $\ell^1$, which is norm compact, and read off uniformly small tails.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The Mackey topology is the norm topology on a Banach space, and the equivalent form for a weakly countably additive [vector measure](c:vector-measure) follows by taking $x_n$ to be the values on disjoint sets.

roles.why: The dual $X^*$ separates points, so weak limits are unique, and the Mackey topology is defined by weak*-compact disks in $X^*$.
Weak subseries convergence makes each scalar series absolutely convergent and gives the limits $x_B$ that define the map into $\ell^1$.

steps.slogan: Show that each functional gives an absolutely convergent scalar series.
steps.detail: For $x^* \in X^*$ and every $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ the series $\sum_{n\in A}\langle x^*, x_n\rangle$ converges. Taking $A$ to be the set where the real part is positive, then negative, and the same for the imaginary part, gives $\sum_n |\langle x^*, x_n\rangle| < \infty$. So $Ux^* = (\langle x^*, x_n\rangle)_n$ lies in $\ell^1$.

steps.slogan: Show that $U$ is bounded on the Banach space spanned by a weak*-compact disk $K$.
steps.detail: Let $K \subseteq X^*$ be absolutely convex and $\sigma(X^*, X)$-compact. Its span $X^*_K$ with the gauge norm is a Banach space. The map $U\colon X^*_K \to \ell^1$ has a closed graph, because coordinates are continuous, so it is bounded.

steps.slogan: Show that $U(K)$ is weakly compact in $\ell^1$.
steps.detail: For $B \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, $\langle Ux^*, \chi_B\rangle = \langle x^*, x_B\rangle$, which is $\sigma(X^*, X)$-continuous in $x^*$. Simple functions are dense in $\ell^\infty$ and $U(K)$ is bounded in $\ell^1$, so $x^* \mapsto \langle Ux^*, a\rangle$ is continuous on $K$ for every $a \in \ell^\infty$. The compact set $K$ maps onto a weakly compact set.

steps.slogan: Use the Schur property of $\ell^1$ to get norm compactness of $U(K)$.
steps.detail: By the Eberlein-Smulian theorem every sequence in $U(K)$ has a weakly convergent subsequence. By Schur's theorem, weak convergence of sequences in $\ell^1$ is norm convergence. So $U(K)$ is norm compact, hence $\sup_{x^*\in K}\sum_{n>N}|\langle x^*, x_n\rangle| \to 0$ as $N \to \infty$.

steps.slogan: Turn the uniformly small tails into convergence in the Mackey topology.
steps.detail: Given $\varepsilon > 0$ choose $N$ with tails below $\varepsilon$ on $K$. For every $A$, $\sup_{x^*\in K}\big|\langle x^*, x_A - \sum_{n\in A, n\le N} x_n\rangle\big| = \sup_K\big|\sum_{n\in A, n > N}\langle x^*, x_n\rangle\big| \le \varepsilon$. The Mackey topology is uniform convergence on such $K$, so the partial sums converge to $x_A$.

concepts.c:locally-convex-space: The dual of the space separates points, which makes weak limits unique.
concepts.c:weak-topology: The hypothesis is convergence in the weak topology, which the proof upgrades.
concepts.c:series: Subseries convergence of the given series is both the hypothesis and the conclusion.
concepts.c:vector-measure: Countable additivity of a vector measure is the same statement for sums over disjoint sets.
